sections.heading: The Pop-Up Alternative
content: If you missed the sold-out workshop, Haricot Vert is running a pop-up at Annabelle's Book Club LA from August 27 through 28, open 11am to 6pm. You can walk in and customize your own Haricot Vert creation without needing a workshop ticket.

The pop-up gives you access to the same Picto-Charms and materials, just in a self-guided format rather than the instructor-led workshop. It is a solid fallback if the workshop sold out before you could register. The pop-up also lets you browse the full Haricot Vert collection beyond what the workshop focuses on.

Annabelle's Book Club LA is a bookshop and cultural space on Ventura Boulevard, and hosting the pop-up there ties the crafting experience back to the book that inspired it. If you are in Studio City anyway, it is worth a visit even if you are not buying anything.

sections.heading: The Broader Charmed Tour
content: This LA date is one stop on Kelsey Armstrong's Charmed book tour. The same workshop format appears in other cities—Austin gets its version on August 30 at Roommate Collective—so if you are in Texas or have travel flexibility, there are additional opportunities to attend.

Craftnook, the community arm of Haricot Vert's Williamsburg, Brooklyn base, is behind the organizing. Their workshop series focuses on accessible, hands-on craft sessions that pair a creative project with conversation and community, which gives these events a relaxed social texture beyond just making a thing.

The combination of book author, craft brand, and community space is a smart way to do a book tour. Instead of a traditional reading and signing, Kelsey gets two hours of hands-on time with her audience, which makes for a more memorable and personal connection than a standard bookstore appearance.

luma-evt-CUx7hOecWJrO8RW.summaryLead: Roommate Collective in Austin hosts the second Charmed workshop stop with author Kelsey Armstrong on August 30-31, offering the same hands-on keychain-making format and signed book that sold out in Los Angeles.

sections.heading: Austin's Turn at the Keychain Bench
content: After the Los Angeles stop sold out, Austin gets its chance. The workshop lands at Roommate Collective on Springdale Road on August 30, with the event running from 6:30pm to 8:30pm local time. The format mirrors the LA version: you build a custom keychain while Kelsey Armstrong talks about her book Charmed, creativity, and running a handmade business.

Roommate Collective is a creative space in East Austin, and the workshop fits the venue's community-oriented programming. You will work with the same Haricot Vert materials—Picto-Charms, vintage findings, jewelry chain, and all the hardware—to assemble a keychain that is entirely your own design.

The space itself is worth noting. Roommate Collective at 1023 Springdale Road is set up for exactly this kind of hands-on gathering, with the room layout and atmosphere to support a group crafting session. If you have been to other events there, you know the venue works well for intimate, interactive experiences.

sections.heading: Tickets and Materials
content: Your ticket includes a signed copy of Charmed, two Picto-Charms, a curated selection of jewelry chain, charms, and trinkets, plus all clasps and jump rings. Guided instruction is built in, and no prior crafting experience is needed. You leave with a finished keychain and a book.

This event is also sold out. The no-cancellation, no-refund policy means any last-minute openings would need to come through the organizers directly. Check the Luma listing for waitlist or transfer options. The sold-out status across both LA and Austin suggests the Charmed tour has real momentum.

The materials are prepared in advance based on confirmed headcount, which is why the cancellation policy is strict. It is a small-team operation, and every ticket represents materials purchased and staffing arranged. That is worth understanding before you register, not after.

sections.heading: The Austin Pop-Up
content: Before the workshop, Haricot Vert runs a pop-up at Roommate Collective from August 29 through 30, open noon to 6pm. You can walk in and customize your own Haricot Vert creation without a workshop ticket, using the same Picto-Charms and materials available at the instructor-led sessions.

The pop-up is a good option if you want the Haricot Vert experience without committing to the full workshop format, or if you want to preview the materials before the workshop begins. It also gives you a chance to browse the broader Haricot Vert collection and see what kinds of designs other people are making.

Roommate Collective's programming tends toward creative and community-focused events, so the pop-up fits naturally into their space. If you are in East Austin on August 29 or 30, the pop-up is easy to visit without any advance planning.

sections.heading: Tour Context and Organizer
content: This Austin date is the second stop on Kelsey Armstrong's Charmed book tour workshop series. The same format runs in Los Angeles on August 29 at Annabelle's Book Club LA, so if you have friends in both cities, the experience is consistent across stops.

Craftnook, the community arm of Haricot Vert's Williamsburg, Brooklyn base, organizes these workshops. Their programming emphasizes accessible, beginner-friendly craft sessions that pair hands-on making with author conversation, which gives the evening a social dimension beyond just the project.

The tour structure—multiple cities, consistent format, pop-up companion events—is well planned for a book launch. It maximizes the number of people who can interact with the materials and the author while keeping the experience intimate enough to feel personal rather than industrial.

luma-evt-cOrVXkSQSbRfWAo.summaryLead: Artverse Gallery in Paris closes its KOY NO YOKAN exhibition by artist POLYGON1993 with a free finissage on September 3, featuring the artist and curator Arthemort for the final walkthrough.

sections.heading: The Closing Reception
content: A finissage is the last chance to see an exhibition before it comes down, and this one brings you into Artverse Gallery for the final moments of KOY NO YOKAN, a show by POLYGON1993 curated by Arthemort. The event runs September 3 from 5pm to 6pm at Artverse Gallery on Rue de Beauce in the Marais.

The gallery describes this as a chance to share those last memorable moments with the artist and curator. For anyone who saw the exhibition during its run or missed it entirely, this one-hour closing is the final opportunity to experience the work in the space it was made for.

The finissage format is deliberately brief—just one hour. That makes it easy to fit into an evening, and it signals that the event is about presence and atmosphere rather than a formal presentation. Show up, see the work one last time, and talk to the people who made it.

sections.heading: POLYGON1993 and the Exhibition
content: POLYGON1993 is the artist behind KOY NO YOKAN, and the exhibition has drawn a crowd—80 people are already marked as going on the Luma listing, with notable names like Brian Beccafico and Relavil Rodford among the confirmed attendees. The title references a Japanese concept about the anticipation of something before it arrives, which suggests the work engages with expectation and timing.

Arthemort curated the show, and their presence at the finissage gives you a chance to hear directly about the curatorial decisions, the artist's process, and the themes running through the exhibition. This is not a formal talk—it is a closing reception where conversation happens naturally.

The combination of the artist and curator both being present makes this more than a standard gallery closing. You get two perspectives on the work, which adds depth to whatever you already know about the exhibition from seeing it or reading about it.

sections.heading: Artverse Gallery and the Venue
content: Artverse is a digital art gallery and culture hub in central Paris, located at 5 bis Rue de Beauce in the 3rd arrondissement. The gallery positions itself at the intersection of digital culture and traditional exhibition space, which fits a show like KOY NO YOKAN.

The venue also hosts its own programming and events beyond exhibitions. If you are visiting Paris and interested in digital art and culture, Artverse is worth following for future events beyond this finissage. Their contact email is available on the listing if you want to inquire about hosting your own event there.

The Marais location puts you in one of Paris's most walkable neighborhoods, so you can combine the finissage with dinner or drinks nearby. The 3rd arrondissement has no shortage of options for extending the evening after the gallery closes.

sections.heading: Registration and Attendance
content: Registration is free and handled through the Luma listing. Given that 80 people are already confirmed and the gallery is not a large space, arriving early is worth your time if you want a comfortable spot.

The event is listed under Arts and Culture on Luma and featured in the Paris category, which means it is getting visibility beyond just the gallery's own audience. If you are in Paris on September 3 and interested in digital art, this is a low-commitment, high-reward way to spend an hour.

ArtVerse also has a presence as a featured organizer on Luma, so following their page will keep you updated on future exhibitions and events at the gallery. The digital art scene in Paris is active, and Artverse is a consistent node in that network.

luma-evt-d4RWCD4h0jfI1C2.summaryLead: Part Three of the R³ Group Bodywork Series at Pluto in Toronto focuses on shoulders, chest, neck, jaw, and head—areas tied to communication, expression, and how you show up in pressure moments.

sections.heading: The Upper Body Focus
content: This is the third installment of Lisa Nogueira's A New Way Forward series, and it moves up the body to the shoulders, chest, neck, jaw, and head. These are the areas involved in expression, communication, and how you respond to what is happening around you. The session explores what happens physically when it is time to speak, be seen, or take up more space.

You may notice your shoulders tightening, your jaw clenching, or tension building through your neck and head in moments of pressure. The workshop treats these patterns as worth examining—not as problems to fix, but as information about how your body relates to communication and connection in everyday situations.

The framing is important here. The organizers are careful to say these are not fixed meanings assigned to body parts. They are reference points for noticing how physical patterns may relate to the way you communicate, relate, and respond. That distinction keeps the work grounded rather than speculative.

sections.heading: What You Will Do
content: The session combines self-bodywork, movement, awareness exercises, and reflection. Most of the work is guided and done on your own body, though hands-on support may be offered and is always optional. You remain fully clothed throughout, and no previous bodywork experience is required.

Themes explored include expression and communication, being seen and taking up space, holding back or over-controlling, carrying responsibility through the upper body, and allowing more choice in how you show up. The session is designed to give you tools you can continue using outside of the room.

The two-hour format is long enough to go deeper than a quick workshop but short enough to maintain focus. You are supported to work at your own pace, which means the experience scales to wherever you are in your body awareness practice.

sections.heading: The Three-Part Series
content: Part One on August 18 covered feet, legs, hips, and pelvis. Part Two on August 27 addressed the core, diaphragm, ribs, and mid-back. Part Three on September 3 completes the arc with the upper body. You can attend any single session, but the three-part structure builds a progressive understanding of how different body regions relate.

Each session runs two hours at Pluto, a community space at 60 Sumach Street in Toronto. The venue is described as a fourth space for community, co-creation, and coworking, which fits the group-oriented, experiential format of the bodywork sessions.

The series design is thoughtful. Starting from the ground up—feet and legs first, then core, then upper body—follows a logical progression that mirrors how body awareness typically develops. Even if you only attend one session, the individual workshops are designed to stand alone.

sections.heading: What to Bring and Ticket Details
content: Wear comfortable clothing you can move in and bring a pillow for additional support. The work is experiential and educational, designed to give you tools you can continue using outside the session. You are supported to work at your own pace and notice what is relevant for you.

Ticket options include a standard admission and a Pluto member rate that requires approval. Nine people are already confirmed to attend, and the event is organized by R³ Group Bodywork, which specializes in group experiences that help people work with the body and shift familiar patterns.

Lisa Nogueira hosts and facilitates the session. Her approach to group bodywork emphasizes individual agency within a shared container—you are not being adjusted or fixed, you are exploring your own patterns with guidance and support. The small group size keeps the experience personal even in a group setting.

mu-315286722.summaryLead: The final session in Microsoft Reactor Redmond's Fabric series introduces Fabric IQ and MCP Ontology—a semantic layer that lets external agents like Claude, Copilot, and Foundry agents reason against your business data without custom integrations.

sections.heading: The Semantic Foundation for Agents
content: This is the most advanced session in the series. Fabric IQ, which went GA at Build 2026, is the shared context layer that unifies Data Agents, semantic models, and Ontologies across OneLake. The session walks you through what an Ontology in Fabric actually is: entities, relationships, properties, and business rules tied to live data.

The practical payoff is that you can expose your Ontology as an MCP server. Any external agent—Claude, Copilot, agents built on Foundry—can then ground its reasoning in your business semantics without you rewriting integrations for each one. That is a meaningful shift from one-off agent deployments to a reusable semantic infrastructure.

The concept of an Ontology in this context is specific to Fabric. It is not a general knowledge graph or a theoretical construct—it is a governed, data-backed definition of your business domain that lives alongside your actual data in OneLake. That makes it both discoverable and trustworthy for agents that need to understand what your data means, not just what it contains.

sections.heading: Building a Multi-Agent Flow
content: The session builds a complete multi-agent pipeline. An orchestrator queries the Ontology via MCP to understand the business context, then delegates to a Data Agent for the actual data retrieval. The result is a response that is both consistent and governed, because every agent in the chain is anchored to the same semantic definitions.

This is not a theoretical architecture discussion. The organizers walk through the full build, from Ontology setup to MCP exposure to agent orchestration. You see the code and the configuration, which means you can adapt the pattern to your own stack once you leave the session.

The multi-agent approach is worth understanding even if you are not planning to deploy it immediately. As more organizations move toward agentic architectures, having a semantic layer that multiple agents can share becomes a governance advantage. It prevents each agent from developing its own interpretation of what your business data means.

sections.heading: Adoption Roadmap and Q and A
content: The session closes with a practical adoption roadmap: what is GA, what is still in Preview, and how to plan for rolling Fabric IQ into your organization. That kind of honest status breakdown is useful for teams trying to decide whether to invest now or wait for broader feature coverage.

The final fifteen minutes are reserved for open Q and A, and the organizers encourage you to bring your own use case. If you have a specific architecture question or a data governance challenge you want to pressure-test, this is the time to do it with people who know the platform deeply.

Bringing your actual use case to the Q and A turns a generic session into a targeted consultation. The organizers have seen enough implementations to give you practical feedback on whether your approach is realistic, what pitfalls to watch for, and where the current feature set might fall short.

sections.heading: Series Context and Access
content: This is the third and final session in the Fabric MCP series at Microsoft Reactor Redmond. The first session on August 28 covered Real-Time Intelligence MCP and streaming data queries. This closing session takes the furthest step toward enterprise-grade agent infrastructure.

The session runs online on September 4, 2026, starting at 8:00 AM Pacific. It is free to attend through Meetup, and the Microsoft Reactor Redmond page has the registration link. Spanish-language delivery keeps it accessible for Latin American and Spanish audiences who want practical Fabric training.

If you have attended the earlier sessions in this series, this one ties the previous concepts together and pushes them into the most complex territory. The progression from streaming queries to semantic ontologies maps directly onto how Fabric's capabilities layer on top of each other in production.

luma-evt-P8SOblAuUmAsdt6.summaryLead: A full-day, hands-on workshop in Zürich teaching public administration employees how to work smarter with ChatGPT and other large language models through practical prompt engineering techniques.

sections.heading: What This Workshop Is Actually About
content: Artificial intelligence isn't some abstract concept for Swiss civil servants anymore. It's already showing up in offices across the public sector, and ChatGPT is usually the first tool people encounter. This full-day training at the Technopark in Zürich is built around a simple premise: if you're going to use these tools, you should know how to use them well enough to get real work done.

The session is organized by staatslabor, a Swiss nonprofit whose stated mission is helping the public administration become more innovative and collaborative through new methods and technologies. They're teaming up with AI Bridge, a partner organization that helps institutions prepare for the AI landscape. Together they're running an interactive day of learning that goes beyond surface-level demos.

sections.heading: What You'll Walk Away With
content: The curriculum covers three main areas. First, you'll get a solid grounding in how large language models actually work — not in a way that requires a computer science degree, but enough to understand what these systems can and can't do. That context matters when you're deciding which tasks to hand off to an AI and which ones still need a human eye.

Second, the workshop teaches prompt engineering techniques that go beyond basic queries. You'll practice writing prompts that pull useful, specific answers out of LLMs rather than getting generic output you'd have to rewrite anyway. Third, you apply everything to real administrative scenarios — tasks from your actual workload that could be simplified or sped up with the right approach. The goal isn't to replace judgment; it's to cut down the tedious parts so you can focus on the work that actually matters.

There's also an explicit emphasis on doing all of this within the boundaries of internal guidelines and data protection regulations. Public administration has stricter privacy requirements than most private sector work, and the workshop doesn't ignore that reality.

sections.heading: The Practical Details You Need
content: The workshop runs on Tuesday, September 8, 2026, from 9:15 AM to 5:00 PM at the Technopark in Zürich — specifically at Technoparkstrasse 1, about ten minutes by tram from Zürich Hauptbahnhof. After the formal session wraps up, there's an apéro where participants can meet each other and the staatslabor community informally.

The price is CHF 650 per person, excluding VAT. Payment options include credit card, debit card, or invoice. The course runs with a minimum of 6 and maximum of 20 participants, so it stays small enough for genuine interaction. Spots are filled on a first-come, first-served basis, and the page notes that only one spot remained at time of writing.

sections.heading: Who This Is For (and Who It Isn't)
content: This workshop is exclusively for employees of public administration. Staatslabor reserves the right to reject registrations from people who don't meet that criteria, so don't sign up if you're in the private sector hoping for a nice day out in Zürich.

Every registration is binding and commits you to paying the course fee. If you can't make it, you need to inform staatslabor proactively before the program starts. If the minimum enrollment isn't met, the course gets canceled and fees are fully refunded. It's straightforward, no-nonsense terms — which honestly tracks for a program run by and for the Swiss public sector.

luma-host-evt-u8z3itUrY0D0LaN.summaryLead: Light DAO's monthly virtual town hall brings together 7,000+ conscious entrepreneurs and 1,200+ investors from 16 cities worldwide for ecosystem updates, a beta app launch, and breakout room connections.

sections.heading: Who Light DAO Actually Is
content: Light DAO describes itself as a global community of conscious entrepreneurs and investors. That word 'conscious' is doing real work in their mission statement — they're focused on what they call expanding collective consciousness and co-creating a regenerative future for humanity. Whether that language resonates with you or makes you skeptical probably depends on where you sit, but the numbers behind it are concrete: over 7,000 entrepreneurs and 1,200 investors across 16 cities in North America, South America, Europe, the Middle East, Asia, and Australia.

This isn't a crypto bro operation running on vibes alone. They have a structured membership system with two tiers — Dao Guest access for qualified investors and experienced founders, and Dao Member Owner status that grants access to both virtual and in-person gatherings across their 16-city network.

sections.heading: What's on the September Agenda
content: The September 9 town hall has a packed agenda. They're opening with a global ecosystem overview, which means updates on what's happening across their various city chapters and initiatives. Then there's a rundown of upcoming gatherings and community events — essentially a calendar preview so members know what's coming.

The headline item is the beta launch of the Light app, which is clearly something the organization has been building toward. Beyond that, there's a stewardship overview, presentations from mastermind teams that focus on deeper collaboration, and global member highlights that spotlight what people in the network are actually building. The session closes with a group connection experience in breakout rooms, which sounds like the structured networking portion where attendees get paired for focused conversations.
The whole thing runs from 6:00 to 7:00 PM on a single evening, keeping it tight. For a monthly recurring event, that brevity is smart — it respects people's time while still covering a lot of ground.

sections.heading: Membership Tiers and Access
content: Getting into the town hall requires either Dao Guest or Dao Member Owner registration, and both tiers require approval. Guest access is for qualified investors and experienced founders, while Member Owner status opens up the full range of Light DAO gatherings — virtual and in-person — across all 16 cities.

At the time of writing, 41 people were already registered as going, with names like Patrick Meagher and Evan Arteaga among them. The approval process suggests they're curating the room deliberately, which makes sense for a community built around 'conscious' entrepreneurship. They're not trying to fill a stadium; they're building a network with specific criteria.

sections.heading: The Virtual Format and Global Reach
content: Holding the town hall virtually makes sense for an organization that spans six continents. A single in-person event in any one city would exclude most of the network, so the virtual format is essentially the only way to get everyone in the same room simultaneously.

The breakout room component is the interesting part — virtual networking at scale is notoriously difficult, but structured breakout sessions at least create the conditions for real one-on-one or small-group conversations. Whether those conversations turn into meaningful collaborations is up to the participants, but the format gives them a fighting chance.

luma-evt-mBERNwQdX2gmBia.summaryLead: A 45-minute strength and endurance fitness class in Los Angeles that pairs functional training with community — plus a complimentary cafecito from Ülew for every attendee.

sections.heading: The Class Itself
content: This isn't a CrossFit gauntlet or a boutique cycling class with a DJ. It's a 45-minute strength and endurance session designed for all fitness levels, focused on functional movements — the kind that make carrying groceries, climbing stairs, and playing with your kids easier. The emphasis is on building real-world strength, improving cardio endurance, and getting people to leave feeling more capable than when they arrived.

Hosted by Metztli Garcia in Los Angeles, the class explicitly invites all levels. Whether you're someone who's never lifted a weight or you're a regular gym-goer looking for a different format, the framing is the same: show up, move your body, and feel stronger afterward. There's no mention of specific equipment or advanced requirements, which keeps the barrier to entry low. The workout targets both strength and endurance in a single session, which means you're not just lifting heavy things or just running on a treadmill — you're getting a balanced push that tests multiple energy systems in under an hour.

sections.heading: Community as the Main Event
content: Here's what makes this different from booking a class at your local gym: after the workout, everyone gets a cafecito from Ülew included with their ticket. The host explicitly calls out that building community is just as important as building muscle. That framing matters — this isn't a transaction where you pay for exercise and leave. It's structured to create social connection around a shared physical activity. The coffee isn't an afterthought either — it's baked into the ticket price, which means nobody has to awkwardly split a check or wonder whether the host is expecting them to buy their own drink.

The invitation to bring your bestie is part of that same ethos. The event name — 'Strong Looks Good On You, Bestie!' — sets a tone that's encouraging rather than competitive. In a fitness culture that often leans into intensity and transformation narratives, this one leans into warmth and belonging. It's a small detail, but the choice to frame the event around friendship and mutual support rather than competition or personal records tells you something about the kind of environment Metztli Garcia is trying to build.

sections.heading: Logistics and the Waitlist Situation
content: The event is already full. At the time of the listing, 25 people were marked as going, and the registration page offered a waitlist option. If additional spots open up, people on the waitlist get notified. That demand signals real interest in what Metztli Garcia is building.

The cost is $15, payable via Venmo or Zelle (with a specific Zelle tag: boyleheightsbestie). Payment is required before approval — no payment, no registration confirmed. The exact class location in Los Angeles is only revealed after registration, which is a common approach for pop-up fitness events to manage capacity and prevent overcrowding.

sections.heading: Refund Policy and Fine Print
content: Refunds are accepted only if requested at least 48 hours before the event starts. After that window closes, your payment is locked in. It's a simple policy that protects the organizer from last-minute drop-offs while still giving people a reasonable grace period to change their minds.

For $15, this is about as low-risk a social experiment as you can find. You get a workout, a coffee, and a room full of people in Los Angeles who are interested in fitness and community. Whether that turns into lasting friendships or just a good Saturday morning is entirely up to what you make of it.

luma-evt-Dd3eNd55rFmR8bj.summaryLead: A multi-day beginner acting workshop at HAFA Art Studio in Fountain Valley covering camera and theater fundamentals, scene study, and character development — culminating in a certificate and potential casting opportunities.

sections.heading: What the Workshop Covers
content: This is a beginner-level acting workshop spread across six days, totaling 24 hours of instruction. The curriculum is split between acting for camera and acting for theater — two disciplines that share a root but demand very different skills. You'll work through scene study and character development, which means understanding how to break down a script, find a character's motivation, and deliver a performance that feels grounded rather than theatrical.

The workshop is a joint presentation by three organizations: HAFA Art Studio, Starz Studio by Marwa Gabriel, and I Studio by Rafik El Rihany. The involvement of the Hollywood Arab Film Festival/Association (HAFA) as the hosting body connects this workshop to a broader network in the Arab film community. That connection pays off at the end — participants will be considered for future casting opportunities through Starz by Marwa Gabriel, giving the training a direct pathway to professional work. It's not just education for its own sake — there's a tangible professional outcome attached to completion.

sections.heading: The Schedule and Where It Happens
content: The workshop runs from September 14 through September 19, 2026. Monday through Friday sessions run from 6:00 PM to 10:00 PM, and Saturday wraps up with an 11:00 AM to 3:00 PM session. That structure lets working people attend the evening sessions without quitting their day jobs, while the Saturday session provides a natural closing experience. The evening format also mirrors real-world filming and rehearsal schedules, which tend to run late — getting used to performing after a full day of other activities is a useful skill in itself.

All sessions take place at HAFA Art Studio, located at 18386 Brookhurst Street in Fountain Valley, California (ZIP code 92708). Fountain Valley sits in Orange County, about 35 miles southeast of downtown Los Angeles. The studio setting means a more intimate learning environment compared to a large theater or university classroom. For beginners who might feel intimidated by a big institutional space, a studio environment tends to feel more personal and less like you're being graded.

sections.heading: Language and Accessibility
content: The instruction is delivered in English with Arabic support available. That bilingual approach reflects the workshop's roots in the Arab film community and makes the training accessible to a wider range of participants. For Arabic-speaking aspiring actors in Southern California, this removes a significant barrier that often exists in English-dominant acting programs.

Every participant who completes the workshop receives a Certificate of Completion presented by all three partner organizations. It's not just a participation trophy — the certificate is backed by three distinct studios and the Hollywood Arab Film Festival, which gives it weight if you're building a resume or applying to other programs.

sections.heading: Registration, Pricing, and What to Know Before You Sign Up
content: Registration comes with two pricing tiers. Early Bird through August 16 costs $400, and regular registration from August 17 through September 14 is $600. Both tiers are non-refundable and non-transferable, so make sure the dates work before committing. At the time of listing, 14 people were registered and only 2 spots remained. The sharp price jump between early and regular registration — a 50 percent increase — makes a clear case for committing early if you know this is something you want to do.

Spots are filled on a first-come, first-served basis with no waitlist mentioned, which means when they're gone, they're gone. If you're considering this workshop, the early bird pricing saves you $200 and disappears a month before the workshop starts. The combination of 24 hours of instruction, a certificate from three studios, and a pathway to casting considerations makes the $400 early bird price a strong value for serious beginners. For context, a single private acting lesson in Los Angeles typically runs $75 to $150 per hour, so getting 24 hours of group instruction with three studio partners for $400 is a different proposition entirely.

luma-evt-aQiimIN6V6gLF9o.summaryLead: A three-hour program at MIT exploring how AI is reshaping cinema — featuring curated film screenings, filmmaker discussions, industry panels, and networking in Cambridge, Massachusetts on Halloween night.

sections.heading: What This Festival Is
content: The Boston — Silicon Valley AI Film Festival is an extension of an international platform dedicated to the intersection of artificial intelligence and filmmaking. This regional edition, scheduled for October 31, 2026, brings together filmmakers, AI creators, tech innovators, researchers, startup founders, investors, students, and creative professionals for a focused three-hour program at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

The event is hosted by Boston International Media Consulting, Inc. (BIMC), and co-hosted by two MIT student organizations: the Asian Women Development Association (AWDA) and Asian Women Development Plan International (AWDPI). The partnership between a media consulting firm and two MIT student associations reflects the event's dual nature — it's both an industry gathering and an academic exploration of where AI-powered storytelling is heading.

sections.heading: The Program Breakdown
content: The three-hour structure is packed. It opens with remarks, then moves into a curated showcase of AI-assisted and AI-generated films. This isn't a free-for-all screening — the films are selected, which means a curatorial team has decided what's worth showing and in what order. After the showcase, the format shifts to industry panels and roundtable discussions with filmmakers and technology professionals.

An audience Q&A gives attendees direct access to the people making and thinking about AI film. There are also creative-technology presentations or demonstrations, which could range from live AI filmmaking tools to behind-the-scenes looks at production workflows. The program closes with structured networking, giving the 35+ registered attendees a chance to connect with each other and with the featured speakers.

sections.heading: The Topics on the Table
content: The festival explicitly covers a wide range of topics that reflect where the AI-film conversation currently sits. Generative AI and visual storytelling is the big umbrella, but underneath that are more specific threads: AI filmmaking tools and production workflows, emerging video-generation technologies, the tension between human creativity and machine-assisted creation, and the thorny questions around authorship, intellectual property, and responsible AI use.

There's also attention paid to entrepreneurship and innovation in creative technology, plus cross-cultural storytelling in the AI era. That last topic connects to the co-hosts' focus and the international scope of the broader Silicon Valley AI Film Festival. It's not just about what AI can do technically — it's about who gets to tell stories and how cultural perspectives shape the technology.

sections.heading: The Venue and Logistics
content: The event takes place at MIT's campus at 77 Massachusetts Avenue in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The exact room within MIT hasn't been announced yet — registration details and the specific location are noted as forthcoming. The timing on October 31 puts it in the middle of Tough Tech Week, a detail the listing highlights. That scheduling positions the festival within a broader ecosystem of technology and innovation events happening around Boston that week.

The event runs from 2:00 to 5:00 PM EDT, which is early enough that you still have your Halloween evening free. At the time of writing, 35 people were registered as going, with names like Herve Flutto from Sparksense and Prajakta Kalbande among them. Registration is currently open with no mention of a fee, though that could change as the event approaches.

sections.heading: Who Should Show Up
content: This event is most valuable for people who sit at the intersection of film and technology — not just filmmakers curious about AI, and not just technologists curious about film, but people who are actively working at that boundary. luma-evt-c8bSoEY0K3wEXlL.summaryLead: A full-day crypto education camp at Paris La Défense, organized by Nairod Invest and supported by CryptoMondays Paris, covering everything from blockchain basics to hands-on trading workshops.

sections.heading: What This Day Is About
content: CryptoMondays X Nairod Invest Day is a one-day intensive running from 9:00 AM to 6:00 PM on Friday, August 28, 2026, at 25 Quai du Président Paul Doumer in Courbevoie — right at Paris La Défense, accessible via Métro 1, Esplanade de la Défense. The event is organized by Nairod Invest, an organization incubated by CCI Paris, and CryptoMondays Paris is backing it with a featured speaker session.

The format is built around a progression from absolute basics to practical skill-building. The morning starts with understanding blockchain, Bitcoin, and the broader crypto ecosystem — exchanges, wallets, DeFi protocols, and stablecoins. By the afternoon, attendees move into security practices, investment strategies, risk management, and live market analysis. The idea is that you walk in knowing nothing and walk out with a working understanding of how to buy, store, and evaluate a crypto asset.

sections.heading: The Agenda in Detail
content: The program covers a wide spread of topics across the day. Early sessions focus on foundational knowledge: what blockchain technology is, how Bitcoin fits into the picture, and what the various corners of the crypto ecosystem actually do. The middle of the day shifts toward security — protecting your assets, recognizing scams, and understanding the real risks involved in holding digital currencies.

The afternoon gets more hands-on. There are workshops on using an exchange platform and setting up a wallet, plus a session on reading and interpreting crypto market data. The final block walks through building your own investment strategy simulation, where participants work through real scenarios before putting money on the line. A live Q&A wraps things up, giving the group a chance to surface remaining questions. Ksenia Drobyshevskaya from CryptoMondays Paris joins for a special interview session during the day.

sections.heading: Who Should Show Up
content: This event explicitly targets two audiences: people who have never touched crypto and people who already hold positions but want to refine their approach. That breadth is unusual for a crypto meetup — most events either assume baseline knowledge or cater exclusively to veterans. Nairod Invest seems to have designed this day so a complete beginner can follow along without feeling lost, while an experienced holder still gets value from the strategy and analysis workshops.

Places are limited and reservation is required, so registering early through the Luma page is important. The event runs on Friday, which means a full workday commitment, but the payoff is a structured educational experience rather than a casual evening talk. If you have been curious about crypto but unsure where to start, or if you have been trading informally and want to build a more disciplined framework, this is a solid use of a day.

sections.heading: Practical Details Worth Knowing
content: The venue is at Paris La Défense, one of Europe's largest business districts, so there are plenty of dining and transport options nearby. Doors open at 9:00 AM with the program officially starting at 9:30 AM, so arriving early gives you time to settle in. The event runs until 6:00 PM, making it a genuine full-day commitment.

CryptoMondays Paris is the presenting organizer, and the event carries the network's community-driven ethos — accessible, educational, and focused on real participation rather than passive listening. The collaboration with Nairod Invest and CCI Paris adds institutional weight, suggesting the content has been vetted beyond what a typical meetup organizer might produce. If you are in the Paris area and want a structured introduction to crypto investing, this is one of the better options on the calendar for late August.

luma-host-evt-dSVTRTCeQZKE3Ec.summaryLead: A free weekly co-working and learning session in downtown Toronto, hosted by Superteam Canada, where Solana builders gather every Friday to work, connect, and share knowledge.

sections.heading: What Happens at VibeStation
content: Toronto Solana VibeStation runs every Friday from 9:30 AM to 6:00 PM in downtown Toronto. It is organized by Superteam Canada, the community arm focused on growing the Solana ecosystem across the country. The format is straightforward: show up, grab a desk or couch or private room, and spend the day building alongside other people working in web3.

The event is not a typical sit-and-listen meetup. It is designed as an active co-working space with educational programming layered in. Expect workshops, panels, and keynotes covering Solana, DeFi, DAOs, NFTs, and related topics. The content rotates based on what partners and community members bring to the table each week, so the experience shifts depending on when you show up.

sections.heading: The Solana Angle
content: Superteam Canada is specifically focused on growing the Solana ecosystem, so the programming leans toward Solana-native tools, protocols, and projects. If you are building on Solana or thinking about it, this is a place to get direct support from people who know the stack. The event description mentions receiving support and advice from Solana experts, plus open mics and demo days where you can showcase your work.

The community aspect is a big part of the draw. You are not just working alone in a room with other people — the format encourages collaboration, finding team members, and networking with builders who might be working on complementary projects. For someone solo-building a Solana project, showing up consistently to a weekly session like this can be the difference between grinding in isolation and finding the collaborators who help you ship.

sections.heading: Logistics and Registration
content: Attendance is free, but registration through the Luma page is required because the venue has limited capacity. The exact address is revealed after you register, which is a common pattern for Superteam events — it keeps the room from being overrun by walk-ins while maintaining a sense of exclusivity for committed attendees. The venue is described as a downtown co-working space equipped with free drinks and snacks.

There are two ticket tiers: a Standard option and a Members-Only option for Superteam members. If you are not yet a member, the Standard ticket gets you in the door. For ongoing updates, the Solana Canada Telegram group (https://t.me/+Dm3WujI--Go1ZjQ0/SuperteamCAN) is the central communication channel. Since this is a weekly recurring event, you can drop in on a Friday that works for your schedule rather than committing to a single date.

sections.heading: Why This Model Works
content: The VibeStation concept solves a real problem in the web3 space: most crypto events are either too educational (panels with no room to apply what you learn) or too social (drinks and networking with no substance). This format splits the difference by giving you a full day of productive workspace with structured learning woven in. You can spend the morning at a workshop and the afternoon heads-down on your own project, all within the same community environment.

For Toronto's growing web3 scene, having a reliable weekly gathering point matters. It creates consistency — you know where to be every Friday — and that consistency builds the kind of community where real collaborations happen. Whether you are a developer, designer, project lead, or just someone exploring the Solana ecosystem, the low barrier to entry and high ceiling on what you can get out of it make this worth putting on your calendar.

When you are surrounded by other builders, conversations happen naturally, and those conversations often lead to collaborations that would never emerge from a screen.

For Montréal's web3 community specifically, having a reliable weekly gathering point creates the kind of infrastructure that lets a local scene mature. If you are in Montréal and building on or interested in Solana, this is a straightforward way to plug into the ecosystem.

mu-314107814.summaryLead: A monthly online strategy discussion hosted by the Kansas City Business Strategy Group, examining why successful leaders sometimes limit their own growth by thinking too small about what their businesses can become.

sections.heading: The Core Question
content: Are You Thinking Too Small? That is the Question! is a one-hour online session happening Tuesday, September 1, 2026, at 11:30 AM CT. It is hosted by David B. through The International Business Strategy Group, a Kansas City-based Meetup community that meets on the first Tuesday of every month via Zoom. The event tackles a specific problem: why successful leaders often become prisoners of their own success.

The discussion frames this as a pattern rather than an individual failing. When your business is working well, there is a natural tendency to assume that what works today will work tomorrow. The event challenges that assumption by exploring why comfortable beliefs about your current business can quietly destroy valuation over time. It is a strategic conversation, not a tactical one — the focus is on mindset and direction, not on specific tools or frameworks.

sections.heading: How the Group Works
content: The Kansas City Business Strategy Group has a distinctive format. Once a month, members share insights on driving growth and value in their business enterprises. The group is described as diverse and dynamic, drawing from different industries and business stages. Each meeting features a topic that ranges from business planning to personal strategies, and the goal is for every participant to identify information and ideas they can adapt to their own situation.

The group's description emphasizes vulnerability and authenticity as prerequisites for the format to work. Members are expected to put themselves on the line — sharing real challenges, not polished success stories. This creates a space where honest conversation can happen, which is rare in business networking contexts where everyone tends to present their best version. The online format via Zoom makes it accessible to people outside Kansas City as well, though the group's roots are in that community.

sections.heading: The Specific Topics
content: The event description lists three specific threads for this session. First, why successful leaders often become prisoners of their own success — the idea that past achievement can create blind spots about future potential. Second, the danger of believing today's business defines tomorrow's potential — a direct challenge to the assumption that current success guarantees future relevance. Third, why comfortable assumptions quietly destroy valuation — the financial consequence of thinking too small.

These three threads build on each other. The first identifies the pattern, the second explains why it happens, and the third shows what it costs. For business owners and leaders, this is a conversation about the gap between where you are and where you could be if you stopped treating your current reality as the ceiling. The format invites participants to reflect on their own businesses and bring specific examples to the discussion.

sections.heading: Participation and Access
content: The event is online via Zoom, with the meeting link visible to attendees after registration. Registration is through Meetup, which is free to join. The session runs for one hour, which keeps the commitment minimal while still allowing enough time for substantive discussion. Since it happens on the first Tuesday of every month, this is part of an ongoing series rather than a standalone event.

For someone running a business who wants a regular space to think strategically about growth, this format offers something that most business resources do: peer conversation with real accountability. The monthly cadence means you can bring a challenge one month, work on it, and report back the next. The online format removes geographic barriers, so you do not need to be in Kansas City to participate. If you have been running your business on autopilot and suspect you are leaving value on the table, this is an hour-long check-in that might shift your perspective.

luma-evt-SN7UWBBLgEM1tmn.summaryLead: A $10 Women of Customer Success event in Austin exploring how the Forward Deployed Engineer role is reshaping Customer Success, featuring panel discussions and roundtable conversations with Cloudflare participation.

sections.heading: The Shift Being Examined
content: WoCS Austin X Cloudflare: The Forward Deployed Era + CS's Shift to Revenue takes place Wednesday, September 24, 2026, from 6:30 PM to 9:30 PM in Austin, Texas. The event, priced at $10, addresses a structural change happening across tech organizations: the emergence of the Forward Deployed Engineer role and how it is pulling technical implementation work away from Customer Success Managers.

The core question is what happens to the CSM role when hands-on technical delivery moves to a dedicated function. The event argues that the CSM seat is not disappearing — it is being redefined around a different core skill: owning revenue. This is not a theoretical discussion. The description notes that this shift is happening industry-wide, and the evening is designed for CS professionals who need to understand what it means for their careers.

sections.heading: The Format and What You Get
content: The evening moves from a panel discussion into small-group roundtable conversations. The panel features leaders and practitioners who have lived through this restructuring firsthand, including, if confirmed, a Cloudflare team member in a Forward Deployed Engineer or Solutions seat. Having someone from Cloudflare — a company that has been vocal about its Forward Deployed approach — in the room gives attendees a concrete example of what this role looks like in practice.

The roundtable portion is where the real work happens. Attendees break into small groups to discuss where they personally sit in this shift, what they should hand off, what they should hold onto, and how to build the language and instincts of someone who owns a revenue number. Bites and beverages are provided, keeping the atmosphere social while the content stays substantive. The combination of panel and roundtable means you leave with both big-picture understanding and specific, personal next steps.

sections.heading: Who Should Attend
content: The event targets four groups: CSMs and Account Managers figuring out what stays on their plate, CS leaders and Directors/VPs who already own or are being asked to own a revenue number, RevOps and CS Ops professionals thinking about team design, and anyone in a post-sales role watching their organization create Forward Deployed Engineer or Solutions Consulting seats. That is a broad but coherent audience — everyone in the room is navigating the same structural shift from a different vantage point.

Women of Customer Success is the organizing community, and the event is built for women working in tech and post-sales roles. WoCS operates with over 10 chapters worldwide, and this Austin edition is part of their broader mission to connect, educate, and empower women in post-sales leadership. The community aspect matters here because the shift being discussed is not just technical — it is career-defining, and having a peer group navigating the same transition adds a support layer that a generic tech event would not provide.

sections.heading: Why This Conversation Is Timely
content: The Forward Deployed Engineer role has gained significant traction in recent years, particularly at companies with complex technical products that require hands-on implementation. As these roles proliferate, the boundary between Customer Success and technical delivery is shifting in real time. CSMs who used to own the full post-sales lifecycle — from onboarding through technical setup to ongoing relationship management — are finding that the technical pieces are being peeled off into dedicated functions.

This creates both opportunity and anxiety. Opportunity, because CSMs who can own revenue and drive expansion are more strategically valuable than ever. Anxiety, because the skills that defined a successful CSM — technical knowledge, product expertise, hands-on implementation ability — are being redistributed. The WoCS Austin event addresses both sides of that equation, giving attendees a framework for understanding where the role is heading and what they need to build toward over the next year to stay ahead of the shift.
